input.question: Why do spicy foods make your mouth feel hot temperature wise, and why do things like milk help it?
input.ground_truth: Capsaicin is the active ingredient in spicy food and it works by triggering the receptors for burning. Capsaicin is fat soluble so drinking milk, eating sour cream or guacamole helps dilute the capsaicin; drinking water is like throwing water on a grease fire -- it usually makes it worse.

response.prediction:
Okay, let’s imagine your mouth is like a playground.

When you eat spicy food, there’s something called “capsaicin” in it. Think of capsaicin like a little firecracker that tricks your mouth. When it touches your tongue, it tells your brain, “Hey! It’s really hot here!” So your brain thinks your mouth is getting hotter, even though it’s not really burning you. That’s why it feels hot!

Now, when you drink milk after spicy food, the milk is like a superhero. The milk has something in it that can help wash away some of those “firecrackers” (the capsaicin) from your tongue. It doesn’t make your mouth colder, but it helps take away the spicy feeling by covering up the capsaicin. So your mouth stops telling your brain it’s hot, and you feel better!
